5588               	;
5589               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5590               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5591               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5592               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5593               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5594               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5595               	; 	'
5596               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5597               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5598               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5599               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5600               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5601               	; 	'
5602               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5603               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5604               	; 	' above it at all.
5605               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5606               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5607               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5608               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5609               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's
5610               	; 	' beams started falling three pixels short.
5611               	; 	'
5612               	; 	' So the roof gets its own version of the stamp. A beam HOLDS THE ROOF
5613               	; 	' UP and must reach it; the shaft merely stops beneath it.

6121               	; 			' lk = OB_BALL`, one per kind -- a hazard that had not
6122               	; 			' arrived was DOWNGRADED TO A BEACH BALL rather than

6127               	; 			' floors". On Krook 1 the radio, cart and plane all became

6129               	; 			' so both carried one on every populated screen forever.
6130               	; 			' It was provable from the gates, not a tuning accident.
6131               	; 			' The original shows a MEDIAN OF ZERO hazards on level 1.
6132               	; 			'

6134               	; 			' write 0 -- which is the thing the gates could not say.)

6389               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6390               	; 			'
6391               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6392               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6393               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6394               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6395               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6396               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6397               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6398               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6399               	; 			'
6400               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6401               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6402               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6403               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6404               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6405               	; 			'
6406               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6407               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6408               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6409               	; 			'
6410               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6411               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is

6413               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off

6603               	; 		' ------------------------------------------- the THIRD radio
6604               	; 		' Past the two table slots the band has one more, at 8+llv, and
6605               	; 		' it is A RADIO OR NOTHING. Its kind does NOT come from the
6606               	; 		' table: the two bytes for slot 2 are still there and still
6607               	; 		' skipped, so the six-byte stride and every placement in
6608               	; 		' store.bas are untouched.
6609               	; 		'
6610               	; 		' It is synthesised from the band's own slot 0 instead -- a
6611               	; 		' third radio appears only where that band already has radios,
6612               	; 		' which is what "a floor carries one, two or three of them"
6613               	; 		' means. Reading a kind out of the table here would have let a
6614               	; 		' third BALL through, and a third ball is a fifth sprite on the
6615               	; 		' scanline, the one thing the two-slot cap exists to prevent.
6616               	; 		'
6617               	; 		' Krook 8, measured: assets/ref2600/hazards.md counts the
6618               	; 		' original's radios at three fixed positions and finds the third
6619               	; 		' arriving two rounds after the second.
6620               	; 		'
6621               	; 		' ONLY THE FIELDS THAT ARE EVER READ BACK are written. obd, obh,
6622               	; 		' obp and obc are write-only at 8-11 -- draw_obst and the
6623               	; 		' obstacle update both stop at 7, and coll_obst reads obh only
6624               	; 		' for a BALL, which this slot can never hold. obht IS read: it
6625               	; 		' is the hit refractory, and a stale one carried across a screen

7677               	; 	' --- running
7678               	; 	' THE END WALLS ARE MOVEMENT LIMITS, NOT A CLAMP APPLIED AFTERWARDS.
7679               	; 	'
7680               	; 	' They used to be the latter, and that is the whole bug: on screen 7 Kelly
7681               	; 	' walked on to x = 254, the crossing routine then noticed there was no
7682               	; 	' screen 8 and set him to 232 -- a 22 px snap BACKWARDS. He reached the
7683               	; 	' wall and was thrown off it. Testing the limit BEFORE the step means he
7684               	; 	' arrives at the wall and stays there, which is what a wall does.
7685               	; 	' IN THE AIR HE IS BALLISTIC. The horizontal direction is fixed at
7686               	; 	' take-off and the stick is ignored until he lands: steering in mid-air
7687               	; 	' is not a jump, it is flight, and it also let him flip which way he was
7688               	; 	' facing halfway through an arc. kjdx is 0 for a standing jump, 1 for a
7689               	; 	' running one to the right, 2 to the left.

8851               	; 	'
8852               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8853               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8854               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8855               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8856               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8857               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8858               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8859               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8860               	; 	' merged object.
8861               	; 	'
8862               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8863               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8864               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8865               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8866               	; 	'
8867               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8868               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8869               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8870               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8871               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8872               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8873               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8874               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8875               	; 	'
8876               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8877               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8878               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
8879               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
8880               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
8881               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
8882               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
8883               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
8884               	; 	' its bottom half together.
8885               	; 	'
8886               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
8887               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
8888               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
8889               	; 	#if NES
8890               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
8891               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
8892               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
8893               	; 	'
8894               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
8895               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
8896               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
8897               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
8898               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
8899               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
8900               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
8901               	; 	'
8902               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
8903               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
8904               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
8905               	; 	'
8906               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
8907               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
8908               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
8909               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
8910               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
8911               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
8912               	; 	'                   the whole time.
8913               	; 	'
8914               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
8915               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
8916               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
8917               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
8918               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
8919               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
8920               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
8921               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
8922               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
8923               	; 	'
8924               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
8925               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
8926               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
8927               	; 	' they only need setting once.
8928               	; 	'
8929               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
8930               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
8931               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
8932               	; 	' as him changing pose.
8933               	; nes_swp16:
8934               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
8935               	; 	'
8936               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
8937               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
8938               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
8939               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
8940               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
8941               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
8942               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
8943               	; 	'
8944               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
8945               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
8946               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
8947               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
8948               	; 	'
8949               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
8950               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
8951               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
8952               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
8953               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
8954               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
8955               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
8956               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
8957               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
8958               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
8959               	; 	ASM JSR nes_suitcases
8960               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
8961               	; 	ntab = 0
8962               	; 	#ncol = 0
8963               	; 	nink = 1
8964               	; 	ncnt = 4
8965               	; 	WAIT
8966               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8967               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
8968               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8969               	; 	WAIT
8970               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8971               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
8972               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
8973               	; 	WAIT
8974               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
8975               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32

8981               	; nes_def_raw:

8983               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrraw
8984               	; 	RETURN
8985               	;
8986               	; nes_def:
8987               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
8988               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
8989               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
8990               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
8991               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
8992               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
8993               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
8994               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
8995               	; 	RETURN
8996               	;
8997               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
8998               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
8999               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
9000               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9001               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
9002               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
9003               	; 	'
9004               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
9005               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
9006               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
9007               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
9008               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9009               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9010               	; 	'
9011               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9012               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
9013               	; nes_escd:

9015               	; 	RETURN

9779               	; 	' that kind's speed, so three calls a pass serve all eight slots.

9821               	; 	' THE BOUNCE PHASE, ON THE SAME CLOCK AS THE JUMP AND AT ITS OLD PERIOD.

9824               	; 	' the bounce advanced once per PASS -- so whether a jump cleared a ball
9825               	; 	' depended on how busy the screen was, and the frame-by-frame property
9826               	; 	' checkball.py proves was exact only at fdv = 1.
9827               	; 	'
9828               	; 	' Stepping the phase by fdv directly would fix the clock and wreck the
9829               	; 	' game: a 32-phase arc would drop from about 1.35 s to 0.55 s, balls
9830               	; 	' bouncing 2.4x faster everywhere. So it gets a fraction of its own --
9831               	; 	' 25/64 of a phase per frame is 23.4 phases a second, against the 23.8 it
9832               	; 	' runs at today. Same bounce, now the same clock as the thing that has to
9833               	; 	' clear it.

10098               	;
10099               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10100               	; 	'
10101               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10102               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10103               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10104               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10105               	; 	'
10106               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10107               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10108               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10109               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10110               	; 	'
10111               	; 	' Three drains support up to 192/64 units per frame. The remainder
10112               	; 	' is below 64, so the byte addition cannot exceed 255. Planes use
10113               	; 	' two-pixel units and double the result outside this shared routine.
10114               	; 	' Other actors retain pixel units and their existing movement rates.
10115               	; 	'
10116               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10117               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10118               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10119               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10120               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10121               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.
10122               	; pace_step:
10123               cvb_PACE_STEP

10626               	;
10627               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10628               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10629               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10630               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10631               	; 	' runs every pass.
10632               	; 	'
10633               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10634               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10635               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10636               	; 	'
10637               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10638               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10639               	; 	'
10640               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10641               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10642               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10643               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10644               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10645               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10646               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10647               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10648               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10649               	; 	'
10650               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10651               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10652               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10653               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10654               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10655               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10656               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10657               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
10658               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
10659               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played
10660               	; 	' the run cycle and did not travel a pixel. He stood at the foot of the
10661               	; 	' flight looking busy.
10662               	; 	'
10663               	; 	' TWO THINGS END THE RUN, AND BOTH ARE VISIBLE ON SCREEN.
10664               	; 	'
10665               	; 	' THE KOP ARRIVING ON THIS FLOOR OUTRANKS IT. This used to override the

10667               	; 	' heading no matter where Kelly was -- and ran straight into him without
10668               	; 	' appearing to notice he was there. The flee above has already worked out

10758               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10759               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10760               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10761               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10762               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10763               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10764               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10765               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10766               	; 	'
10767               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10768               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10769               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10770               	; 	'
10771               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10772               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10773               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10774               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10775               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10776               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10777               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10778               	; 	'
10779               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10780               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10781               	; 	'
10782               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10783               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10784               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10785               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10786               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10787               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10788               	; 	'
10789               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10790               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10791               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10792               	; 	' before any of this.
10793               	; 	'
10794               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10795               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10796               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10797               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10798               	; 	' journey.
10799               	; 	'
10800               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10801               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10802               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.

11263               	;
11264               	; 	' ======================================================================
11265               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11266               	; 	' ======================================================================
11267               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11268               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11269               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11270               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11271               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11272               	; 	'
11273               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11274               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11275               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11276               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11277               	; 	' broken.
11278               	; 	'
11279               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11280               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11281               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11282               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11283               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11284               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11285               	; 	'
11286               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11287               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11288               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11289               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11290               	; coll_obst:
11291               cvb_COLL_OBST

11754               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11755               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11756               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11757               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11758               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11759               	; 	' away from.
11760               	; 	'
11761               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
11762               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
11763               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
11764               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
11765               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --
11766               	; 	' and it left the one hazard that cannot leave on its own as the only one
11767               	; 	' the mercy did not cover. haz_off now takes the characters with it.
11768               	; 	'
11769               	; 	' NOTHING RESTORES IT HERE. load_band repopulates the band from the
11770               	; 	' template, and it runs only on a seam crossing or a round start, so
11771               	; 	' "until the screen is re-entered" costs no state and no timer: leave and
11772               	; 	' come back and the hazards are simply placed again.
11773               	; 	'
11774               	; 	' THE CALL ITSELF IS IN THE MAIN LOOP, at the end of the freeze -- see
11775               	; 	' the hfz block there for why.
11776               	; 	' A HIT DOES NOT END A JUMP. This used to force ST_RUN and zero the arc,
11777               	; 	' which dropped him straight down out of mid-air onto whatever he happened
11778               	; 	' to be over -- and since the arc is ballistic and ignores the stick once
11779               	; 	' he is airborne (0l), that read as the game taking the controls away
11780               	; 	' rather than as a hit landing. The penalty is the nine units and the
11781               	; 	' hit sound; where he comes down is still his own arc.

11943               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11944               	; 	'
11945               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11946               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11947               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11948               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11949               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11950               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11951               	; 	'
11952               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11953               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11954               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11955               	; 	'
11956               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
11957               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
11958               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
11959               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11960               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11961               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
11962               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.
11963               	; 	hva = 0

13145               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13146               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table

13148               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13149               	; 	'

13151               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13152               	; 	'
13153               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13154               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13155               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13156               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13157               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13158               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13159               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13160               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13161               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13162               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13163               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.

13190               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13191               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13192               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13193               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13194               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13195               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13196               	; 	'
13197               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13198               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13199               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13200               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13201               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13202               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13203               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

13218               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13219               	; 	'
13220               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13221               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13222               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13223               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13224               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13225               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13226               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13227               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13228               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13229               	; 	'
13230               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13231               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13232               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13233               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13234               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13235               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13236               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13237               	; 	'
13238               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13239               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13240               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13241               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13242               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13243               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13244               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13245               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13246               	; 	' with room to spare.
13247               	; 	'
13248               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13249               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13250               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13251               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13252               	; 	WAIT
13253               	; 	#endif
13254               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13255               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13256               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13257               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13258               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13259               	; 	'
13260               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13261               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13262               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13263               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13264               	; 	'
13265               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13266               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13267               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13268               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13269               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are
13270               	; 	' PIXEL-IDENTICAL and are never wanted in the same screen THIRD, so they
13271               	; 	' share their characters now and are told apart by the per-third colour
13272               	; 	' table (see esc_deck_col in setup). Six either side.
13273               	; 	'
13274               	; 	' The handrail and the frame sit past the end of both ranges and never
13275               	; 	' move at all.
13276               	; 	IF klsc = 0 THEN

13605               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually

13902               	; 	' A LEVEL BAND IS SIX PIXEL ROWS ON THE NES AND FOUR ON THE TI.
13903               	; 	'
13904               	; 	' It was six everywhere once. It shrank to four to buy eight empty pixel
13905               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
13906               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
13907               	; 	'
13908               	; 	' On the NES that margin now comes from somewhere else: the name table is
13909               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
13910               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
13911               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,
13912               	; 	' and the instrument goes from 16 pixels tall to 24 -- half again, which is
13913               	; 	' what "not quite so vertically thin" asks for.
13914               	; 	'
13915               	; 	' The TI cannot follow: its name table ENDS at row 23, the scanner is on
13916               	; 	' the last three rows, and there is nowhere to put the margin. So the band
13917               	; 	' height is per-target and every row offset below is derived from it.
13918               	; 	'

13948               	;
13949               	; scan_or1:
13950               cvb_SCAN_OR1
13951               	; 	' THE ONE READ-MODIFY-WRITE ON THE PATTERN TABLE. The radar ORs a
13952               	; 	' pixel row into a canvas character, so it has to know what is already
13953               	; 	' there. On the NES that read comes from nsc, which scan_wipe zeroed
13954               	; 	' and which only this routine writes -- so it is exact, not an
13955               	; 	' approximation of what the PPU holds.
13956               	; 	' AND ON THE NES IT CLEARS RATHER THAN SETS, WHICH IS NOT A TYPO.
13957               	; 	'
13958               	; 	' This routine only ever draws the escalator flights (three call sites,
13959               	; 	' all in scan_escs). On the TI they are drawn as INK and coloured black by
13960               	; 	' scan_escc, so the bits go IN. Here the canvas is wiped to green -- plane
13961               	; 	' 0 set everywhere, see scan_wipe. Black is index 2: clear plane 0 and
13962               	; 	' set plane 1 for the same pixels. Preserve the caller's pattern address.
13963               	; 	'
13964               	; 	' 255 - fm1 is NOT fm1: a byte subtracted from all-ones never borrows, so
13965               	; 	' it is the bitwise complement without needing one.
13966               	; 	#if NES
13967               	; 	#nsi = #sda - #nsb
13968               	; 	sva = nsc(#nsi)
13969               	; 	fmn = 255 - fm1
13970               	; 	sva = sva AND fmn
13971               	; 	nsc(#nsi) = sva
13972               	; 	VPOKE #sda,sva
13973               	; 	#nsi = #nsi + 8
13974               	; 	sva = nsc(#nsi)
13975               	; 	sva = sva OR fm1

14075               	;
14076               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
14077               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
14078               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
14079               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
14080               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
14081               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14082               	; scan_wipe:
14083               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
14084               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
14085               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
14086               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
14087               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
14088               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
14089               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
14090               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
14091               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
14092               	; 	'
14093               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
14094               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
14095               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
14096               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
14097               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
14098               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
14099               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
14100               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
14101               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
14102               	; 	'
14103               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
14104               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
14105               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
14106               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
14107               	; 	'
14108               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
14109               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.

14722               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
14723               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,
14724               	; 	' then uploads all 64 bytes through nes_attrs_put within one vblank.
14725               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES GOLD ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
14726               	; 	' bytes in #nav.

14728               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
14729               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14730               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14731               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14732               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14733               	; 	'
14734               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14735               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14736               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14737               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
14738               	; 	'
14739               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
14740               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,

14742               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
14743               	; 	' these beside it.
14744               	; 	'
14745               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a

15248               	;
15249               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15250               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15251               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15252               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15253               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15254               	; 	'
15255               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15256               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15257               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15258               	; 	'
15259               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15260               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15261               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15262               	; 	'
15263               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15264               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15265               	; 	'
15266               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15267               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15268               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15269               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15270               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15271               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15272               	; 	'
15273               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15274               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15275               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15276               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15277               	; 	'
15278               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15279               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15280               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15281               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
15282               	; bonus_count:

15425               	;
15426               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15427               	; 	'
15428               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15429               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15430               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15431               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15432               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15433               	; 	'
15434               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15435               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15436               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15437               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15438               	; 	' counting stops.
15439               	;
15440               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15441               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15442               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15443               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15444               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15445               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15446               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15447               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15448               	; 	'
15449               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15450               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15451               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
15452               	;

15498               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
15499               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
15500               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
15501               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
15502               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
15503               	; 	'
15504               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
15505               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
15506               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
15507               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
15508               	; 	'
15509               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
15510               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
15511               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
15512               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
15513               	; 	'
15514               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
15515               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
15516               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
15517               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
15518               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
15519               	; 	'
15520               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.

15797               	;
15798               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15799               	; 	'
15800               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15801               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15802               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15803               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15804               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15805               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15806               	; 	'
15807               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15808               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15809               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15810               	; 	'
15811               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15812               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15813               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15814               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15815               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15816               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15817               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15818               	; 	'
15819               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15820               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15821               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15822               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15823               	; 	'
15824               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15825               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15826               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15827               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15828               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15829               	; 	'
15830               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15831               	; 	' did not finish.
15832               	; pause_beat:
15833               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT
15834               	; 	GOSUB snd_pend
15835 F2B4 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F2B6 A980

15840               	; 	' call sites would have cost code to say the same thing worse.
15841               	; 	'
15842               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNT AND NOT THE WAITS. sfx_tick runs once per pass, so it

16264               	;
16265               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16266               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16267               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16268               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16269               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16270               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16271               	;
16272               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16273               	; 	'
16274               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16275               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16276               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16277               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16278               	; 	'
16279               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16280               	; 	'
16281               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16282               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16283               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16284               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16285               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16286               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16287               	; 	'
16288               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16289               	; 	'
16290               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16291               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16292               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16293               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16294               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16295               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16296               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16297               	; 	'
16298               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16299               	; 	'
16300               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16301               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16302               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16303               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16304               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16305               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16306               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16307               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16308               	; 	'
16309               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16310               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16311               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16312               	; 	'
16313               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16314               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16315               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16316               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16317               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16318               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16319               	; 	'
16320               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16321               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16322               	; 	'
16323               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16324               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16325               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16326               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16327               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16328               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16329               	; 	'
16330               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16331               	; 	'
16332               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16333               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16334               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
16335               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
16336               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
16337               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not
16338               	; 	' back to 7.

     F798 F774     
16663               	;
16664               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16665               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16666               	; 	'
16667               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16668               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16669               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16670               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16671               	; 	'
16672               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16673               	; 	'
16674               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16675               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16676               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16677               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16678               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16679               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16680               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16681               	; 	'
16682               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16683               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16684               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16685               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16686               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16687               	; 	'
16688               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16689               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16690               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16691               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16692               	; 	#if TI994A
16693               	; 	BANK 2
16694      0864     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$
     **** ****     > .rept

16974               	; 	'     DEFINE COLOR   0,32,tfont_col0

16976               	; 	'     DEFINE COLOR 185,12,tfont_col1
16977               	; 	'
16978               	; 	' LIVES IN BANK 2 -- read once by those DEFINEs.
16979               	; 	' ==================================================

17600               	; 	' Keystone Kapers art -- GENERATED by assets/genart.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
17601               	; 	'
17602               	; 	' EVERY SPRITE IS 16x16: sprite size and magnification are GLOBAL on the
17603               	; 	' TMS9918, so small objects are drawn small INSIDE a 16x16 box rather than
17604               	; 	' being small sprites.
17605               	; 	'
17606               	; 	' EVERY 8-PX OBJECT SITS IN ROWS 8-15 OF ITS BOX, ducked Kelly included, so
17607               	; 	' one rule places them all: bottom edge = y + 16, and a thing resting on the
17608               	; 	' floor is at y = FLOORY - 16.
17609               	; 	'
17610               	; 	' Sprite bytes are QUADRANT-ORDERED: 16 rows of the left half, then 16 of
17611               	; 	' the right. Every block is an EVEN number of bytes -- an odd DATA BYTE run
17612               	; 	' silently misaligns every word table after it (CLAUDE.md 3A).
17613               	;

18729               	; 	' -------------------------------------------------- scanner canvas
18730               	; 	' Chars 208-255: 16 cols x 3 rows over screen rows 21-23. Blank to start;
18731               	; 	' dots are plotted by VPOKEing the PATTERN table (rows 21-23 sit in the
18732               	; 	' third screen third, so every scanner pattern is at base 4096).
18733               	;
18734               	; 	' --------------------------------------------------- font colours
18735               	; 	' Chars 32-90, EIGHT bytes each. Without this the font keeps whatever
18736               	; 	' CVBasic left in the colour table, which on a green store made the HUD
18737               	; 	' unreadable.
18738               	;
18739               	; esc_deck:	' 6 x (char, 8 colour bytes) -- write into the THIRD-0 colour table at 8192 + char*8, once, at setup
18740               cvb_ESC_DECK

     7190 1A1A

18846               	; 	INCLUDE "store.bas"
18847               	; 	' Keystone Kapers store -- GENERATED by assets/genstore.py. Do not edit.
18848               	; 	'
18849               	; 	' EIGHT band templates of 5 rows x 32 cols (160 bytes each) plus a 32-byte
18850               	; 	' index over (level, screen). The whole 8-screen, 4-level building is about
18851               	; 	' 1.3 KB instead of the 5,120 bytes it would cost to store literally.
18852               	; 	'
18853               	; 	' All eight templates are ONE contiguous block under ONE label, so a band
18854               	; 	' blit is
18855               	; 	'     SCREEN stor_tpl, tpl*160, toprow*32, 32, 5, 32
18856               	; 	' with no label ladder -- SCREEN needs a literal label and a label cannot be
18857               	; 	' chosen by a variable, which is why RallyX needed a 4-way IF over its maze
18858               	; 	' tables. One block sidesteps it.
18859               	; 	'
18860               	; 	' 160 is EVEN, so this cannot leave the location counter odd and misalign
18861               	; 	' the word tables defined after it.
18862               	; 	'
18863               	; 	' template ids:
18864               	; 	'   0 T_AISLE_A
18865               	; 	'   1 T_AISLE_B
18866               	; 	'   2 T_ESC_W
18867               	; 	'   3 T_ESC_E
18868               	; 	'   4 T_ELEV
18869               	; 	'   5 T_ROOF0
18870               	; 	'   6 T_ROOF1
18871               	; 	'   7 T_ROOF2
18872               	; 	'   8 T_ROOF3
18873               	; 	'   9 T_ROOF4
18874               	; 	'   10 T_ROOF5
18875               	; 	'   11 T_ROOF6
18876               	; 	'   12 T_ROOF7
18877               	; 	'   13 T_END_W
18878               	; 	'   14 T_END_E
18879               	;
18880               	; stor_tpl:	' 15 templates x 160 bytes

19496               	;
19497               	; 	' THE SKYLINE'S LAST BAND WITHOUT ITS YELLOW, high nibble ink, low nibble
19498               	; 	' paper, one byte a scan line -- the same shape genart emits into
19499               	; 	' store_col. SKY2 is white-on-9 throughout instead of turning to paper 10
19500               	; 	' at row 4; BLDGL holds its blue one row longer and then meets its own
19501               	; 	' grey wall. Both are the generated bytes with 10 replaced by 9 and
19502               	; 	' nothing else changed. See setup_rest.
19503               	; #if NES
19504               	; nes_sky2c:
19505               	; 	DATA BYTE $F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9,$F9
19506               	; nes_bldlc:
19507               	; 	DATA BYTE $B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$B9,$BE,$BE,$BE
19508               	; #endif
19509               	;
19510               	; 	' THE IN-GAME FONT'S COLOUR, one byte a scan line and eight a character for
19511               	; 	' all 59 of them. $B4 is light yellow on dark blue -- ink index 3, paper index 1 --
19512               	; 	' and which colours those are is then the attribute table's business, per
19513               	; 	' region: dark blue behind the HUD, the store's green behind a message box.
19514               	; 	'
19515               	; 	' 472 bytes of one repeated value. That reads like waste and is the cheap
19516               	; 	' option: ROM is three budgets here and this is not the scarce one, while
19517               	; 	' the alternative is a second font (impossible -- only eleven free codes)
19518               	; 	' or a new uploader parameter (no RAM -- two bytes left).
